source_evidence.anchor: Let X1, X2, ... be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with mean μ and finite variance.
source_evidence.observation: The exercise assumes an infinite identically distributed and independent sequence, a common mean μ, and finite variance.
The requested conclusion concerns the expectation of the absolute deviation of the sample mean from μ, with an asymptotic upper rate of order N^{-1/2}.

binders: A sequence of random variables (X_i) indexed by positive integers
A positive integer sample size N
hypotheses: The random variables X_1, X_2, ... are independent and identically distributed.
The common distribution has finite variance.
conclusions: As N tends to infinity through positive integers, E[|(1/N) Σ_{i=1}^N X_i − μ|] = O(N^{-1/2}).
definitions_and_conventions: The sample mean is (1/N) Σ_{i=1}^N X_i.
The displayed expectation is taken after applying absolute value to the sample-mean error.
Big-O is an asymptotic upper-bound assertion as N → ∞: there exist constants C and N_0 such that for every integer N ≥ N_0, E[|(1/N) Σ_{i=1}^N X_i − μ|] ≤ C/√N.
The Big-O constant may depend on the common distribution, in particular on its finite variance, but not on N.
implicit_context: N ranges over positive integers because it is the number of summands and appears in the denominator.
The random variables are real-valued, as indicated by their mean, variance, summation, subtraction from μ, and absolute value.
Finite variance supplies the integrability needed for the displayed absolute-error expectation.
No positivity assumption on the variance is stated; the zero-variance case is included.

details: Independence applies jointly to the sequence.
Identical distribution gives a common mean and common finite variance.
The absolute value is inside the expectation.
The centered quantity is the sample mean minus the common mean μ.
The claim is not an almost-sure bound and not a bound on the signed expectation.
The required asymptotic rate is N^{-1/2}.
Only an upper Big-O estimate is requested, not a matching lower bound or asymptotic equivalence.
N is positive whenever the sample mean is formed.
The limit N → ∞ is interpreted along the positive integers.

undebatable_constraints: Preserve the assumption that the sequence is i.i.d.
Preserve the existence of a common mean μ.
Formalize the expectation of the absolute sample-mean error, not the absolute value of its expectation.
Use the sample mean with normalization 1/N and sum from i = 1 through N.
State an O(1/√N) upper rate as N → ∞.
Interpret N as a positive integer sample size in the displayed expression and as tending to infinity through integers.
Do not strengthen the conclusion to an exact asymptotic, convergence in distribution, or a lower bound.

ambiguities.issue: The ambient probability space and codomain of the random variables are not explicitly stated.
ambiguities.evidence: The exercise only calls X_i random variables and uses real-valued mean, variance, subtraction, and absolute value.
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must introduce a probability space and will naturally choose real-valued random variables.

ambiguities.issue: The constant hidden by Big-O is not specified.
ambiguities.impact: The formal statement should existentially quantify an N-independent constant; it may depend on the common distribution or variance.

ambiguities.issue: The source does not explicitly spell out that N is positive.
ambiguities.evidence: N occurs as the upper summation limit and in the denominator 1/N, followed by N → ∞.
ambiguities.impact: A formalization should restrict the sample-mean assertion to positive natural N or use an equivalent indexing convention that excludes division by zero.

contract_plain_english: For an infinite sequence of independent, identically distributed real random variables having common mean μ and finite variance, the expected absolute difference between the average of the first N variables and μ is bounded by a constant times 1/√N for all sufficiently large positive integer N.
